definition: Spinning turns fibers into continuous yarn by drafting them to the required fineness and binding them with twist, wrapping or entanglement; the same word also names extruding polymers into filaments.
explanation: In staple-fiber spinning, a prepared strand (sliver or roving) is attenuated by drafting and then consolidated. Ring spinning inserts real twist as a small traveler circles a ring around a rotating spindle, winding the yarn onto a bobbin in the same operation. Rotor, or open-end, spinning opens sliver into individual fibers, feeds them into the groove of a fast-turning rotor and draws off a twisted yarn. Air-jet spinning uses compressed-air vortices so that a mostly parallel core is held together by wrapper fibers. Each route builds a different internal structure, so yarns of the same count can differ in strength, hairiness and hand.
example: A mill compares three cotton yarns of the same count spun from the same bale mix. The ring yarn goes into a fine poplin shirting where strength matters, the rotor yarn into a heavier jersey where evenness and cost matter most, and the air-jet yarn into a knit intended to resist pilling. The fiber is identical; the spinning route changes how each fabric behaves.
caution: Yarn spinning is different from fiber spinning (melt or solution extrusion), which makes the filaments of polyester, nylon or viscose; context decides which is meant. Labels rarely state the spinning route, and 'ring-spun' on its own says nothing about fiber length, yarn count or fabric quality. Rotor and air-jet yarns are not simply inferior; they suit different end uses and yarn counts.
deeper: Ring spinning output is limited by spindle speed and by the traveler, which is dragged around the ring by the yarn, while the rotating balloon of yarn above it limits tension. Rotor spinning separates twisting from package winding, and rotor speeds of up to roughly 140,000 rpm are reported; its yarns carry characteristic belt, or wrapper, fibers around a twisted core. Comparative studies report that ring yarns generally give the highest strength, while rotor yarns show fewer imperfections and better evenness. Rotor spinning is typically more economical in coarse and medium counts, ring spinning in fine counts. Air-jet yarn properties depend on the proportion of core to wrapper fibers.
origins: Hand spinning with a weighted spindle is among the oldest textile technologies, later supplemented by the spinning wheel. Mechanized spinning developed in Britain and the United States during the industrial era, and the ring frame became the standard machine for staple yarn. Rotor spinning entered commercial use in the second half of the twentieth century, followed by air-jet systems; both raise output by separating twist insertion from the rotation of the yarn package.

definition: Super S numbers, such as Super 120s, are designations on worsted wool fabrics that signal the fineness of the wool fibers used, with higher numbers indicating finer fiber.
explanation: The designation is tied to mean fiber diameter in microns, the property that most affects how soft wool feels against skin and how fine a yarn it can make. A Super number is attached to a fabric, not to a sheep, and in principle describes the wool that went into it. Industry codes of practice and, in some jurisdictions, labeling rules link each Super number to a maximum mean diameter and set conditions on its use. Because the current official table could not be checked for this edition, specific micron values are deliberately not given here.
example: Two navy suitings are labeled Super 110s and Super 150s. A buyer expects the second to use finer wool and to feel smoother. The buyer should also expect the finer fabric to be lighter and potentially less resistant to abrasion and creasing. The label says nothing about the weave, yarn twist, finishing or whether the fabric suits daily wear.
caution: A Super number describes fiber fineness only. It does not certify origin, animal welfare, farming method, dyeing quality or durability; very fine fabrics can be more delicate. Whether a Super claim may legally appear, and under what conditions, is a jurisdiction-specific question; in the United States, check the current text of the Wool Products Labeling Act and FTC rules rather than a supplier's summary.
deeper: Wool fineness is measured as mean fiber diameter in microns on a fiber sample, usually with a distribution around the mean; the standard deviation or coefficient of variation matters for handle and prickle. Finer fibers allow more fibers in a yarn cross-section at a given linear density, which permits finer, smoother yarns and lighter cloth. That is the physical reason Super numbers rise as microns fall. Verification requires laboratory measurement of fiber diameter on fibers taken from the fabric or its yarns, compared against the diameter limits in the governing code or regulation. A buyer who needs certainty should request test results rather than rely on the woven selvedge mark.
origins: Super numbers are generally described as descending from the older worsted quality-number tradition, in which finer wool could be spun into higher counts. Over time the number came to be read as a fineness grade rather than an achievable spinning count, and the need for consistency led industry bodies and regulators to define the term. This edition could not confirm the dates and wording of those definitions, so it states the history qualitatively.
